papers.title_in_file: Ensemble-learning error mitigation for variational quantum shallow-circuit classifiers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results on noise-free and noisy VQC, Bagging and AdaBoost sections, conclusions. Appendices and the SPT phase dataset section only skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study proposing Bagging and AdaBoost ensembles of shallow variational quantum classifiers as error mitigation, compared with zero-noise extrapolation.

assertions.value: The authors report that both ensemble-learning protocols, Bagging and AdaBoost, substantially outperform error-mitigated primitive classifiers, and that AdaBoost performs better than Bagging.
quotes: While both of our protocols substantially outperform error-mitigated primitive classifiers, the adaptive boosting shows better performance than the bootstrap aggregating.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against zero-noise extrapolation on a deep circuit under a simulated noise model, not against hardware runs.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in noise-free circuits, AdaBoost VQC with Lc=6 classifiers achieves an accuracy of 0.95, while Bagging VQC even with Lc=10 classifiers cannot exceed 0.92 accuracy.
assertions.anchor: Results, AdaBoost noise-free section, Fig. 4, page 8
quotes: VQC with Lc=6 classifiers can achieve an accuracy of 0.95 while the Bagging VQC even with Lc=10 classifiers cannot exceed 0.92 accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study on an 8x8 digit dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote omits the circuit depth; the surrounding sentence states 3-layer circuits.

assertions.value: The authors report that Bagging with Lc=10 classifiers reaches accuracy 0.8856 (circuit with Dl=2 layers) and 0.9173 (circuit with Dl=3 layers) in noise-free simulation, against 0.9205 for a single circuit with Dl=6 layers.
assertions.anchor: Results, Bagging section, Fig. 2 and Fig. 4(a), page 7
quotes: for Lc=10 one can achieve the accuracy of 0.8856 (for the circuit with Dl=2 layers) and 0.9173 (for the circuit with Dl=3 layers).
To achieve a similar accuracy on a single circuit one needs a quantum circuit with Dl=6 layers (0.9205), see Fig.2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulated study.

assertions.value: The authors state the MNIST subset has 2267 samples, with 1541 used for training and 726 unseen samples used for testing, and that the baseline circuit in the first experiments is noise-free with perfect gates.
assertions.anchor: Results, VQC for classical data, pages 5-6
quotes: The dataset contains 2267 samples from which 1541 samples are used for training and the 726 unseen samples are used for testing the accuracy.
Note that our quantum circuit is noise-free and all quantum gates operate perfectly.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup.
assertions.reader_inference: All results are simulations of a noise model, not runs on real quantum hardware.

papers.title_in_file: Benefits of Open Quantum Systems for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 4 examples (reservoir computing and reinforcement learning), conclusions. Background sections 2 and 3 skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A Perspective review arguing that noise and dissipation can sometimes benefit quantum machine learning, using three prior examples.

assertions.value: The authors state that noise and dissipation can provide substantial advantages in the operation of quantum machine learning algorithms under certain circumstances.
quotes: Surprisingly, it is shown that these seemingly detrimental factors can provide substantial advantages in the operation of quantum machine learning algorithms under certain circumstances.
assertions.certainty_reason: A perspective summarizing other authors' works, not a new result.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper presents three examples drawn from earlier work; none is a general theorem.

assertions.value: The authors report, summarizing prior work, that under specific conditions amplitude damping noise can enhance the performance of quantum reservoir computing, while depolarizing and phase damping channels give poorer outcomes, with depolarizing worse than phase damping.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, quantum reservoir computing example, page 10
quotes: under specific conditions, the presence of amplitude damping noise can enhance the performance of QRC. However, in contrast, both the depolarizing and phase damping channels result in poorer outcomes for QRC, with the depolarizing channel showing even worse performance than the phase damping channel.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that a definitive demonstration of quantum machine learning's efficiency advantage is yet to be achieved, and that further investigation is needed on whether the dissipation benefit in the reinforcement learning example holds with more qubits or in other protocols.
assertions.anchor: Section 1 page 1, and Section 4 reinforcement learning example
quotes: While a definitive demonstration of this capability is yet to be achieved, notable progress is being made in both theoretical and experimental aspects.

However, further investigation is needed to determine whether this assertion holds true for the current protocol when increasing the number of qubits or in other types of quantum reinforcement learning protocols.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope and limits.

papers.title_in_file: The Road to Quantum Artificial Intelligence
papers.what_it_is: A 2007 conference overview of quantum computation basics and speculative ideas for applying it to artificial intelligence problems.

assertions.value: The author claims that quantum computation can reduce time complexity to polynomial range and so eventually provides a more efficient way to address NP-hard AI problems such as scheduling and search.
quotes: In principle, a great deal of the problems that AI attempts to confront is too heavy for classical algorithmic approaches, i.e. NP-hard problems such as scheduling, search, etc.
Since QC can reduce time complexity to polynomial range, it eventually provides a more efficient way to address these problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Quantum computers are not known to solve NP-hard problems in polynomial time; Grover search gives only a quadratic speedup. The claim reads as stronger than established theory.

assertions.value: The author describes Grover's algorithm as searching N=2n items superimposed on a quantum register of n qubits using a certain state as a search key (the superscript n of the exponent is flattened in the extracted text).
quotes: Grover's Algorithm: It searches N=2n items superimposed on a quantum register of n qubits using a certain state as a search key.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Grover 1997).

assertions.value: The author claims that, given the proper hardware, a quantum algorithmic process would be able to solve chess playing in acceptable time.
quotes: Given the proper hardware, a quantum algorithmic process would be able to solve it in acceptable time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No algorithm or complexity argument is given; the claim is speculative.

assertions.value: The author states the paper explains the potential application of quantum computation to traditional AI problems and methods through a very narrow choice of recent papers and research directions.
quotes: This paper attempted to present the basics of QC to readers already familiar with AI, explaining QC's potential application to traditional AI problems and methods through
a very narrow choice of recent papers and research directions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope.

papers.title_in_file: Estimating Quantum Mutual Information Through a Quantum Neural Network
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated February 2024.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, numerical results section, conclusions. Proofs in the main text and appendices skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes QMINE, a quantum neural network method using a quantum Donsker-Varadhan representation to estimate von Neumann entropy and quantum mutual information.

assertions.value: The authors propose a quantum machine learning method called quantum mutual information neural estimation (QMINE) for estimating von Neumann entropy and quantum mutual information.
quotes: We propose a method of quantum machine learning called quantum mutual information neural estimation (QMINE) for estimating von Neumann entropy and quantum mutual information, which are fundamental properties in quantum information theory.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in simulations with N = 4 qubits, they achieved error rates ranging from 0.1% to 1% for each tested random density matrix.
assertions.anchor: Section V, numerical results, QMI estimation, page 7
quotes: We estimated the quantum mutual information of a random density matrix using simulations with N = 4 qubits. For each tested random density matrix, we achieved error rates ranging from 0.1% to 1%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors report in simulation that QMINE converges faster when the rank k of the parameter matrix T equals the rank r of the density matrix than when k > r, and they recommend k = r.
assertions.anchor: Section V.A, rank analysis, Fig. 2, page 6
quotes: These results support the QDVR's claim that the rank of the optimal solution T is r.
Because convergence is faster when k = r than when k > r, it is best to use QMINE with k = r.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one simulation study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the performance of QMINE was demonstrated through numerical simulations of a quantum circuit on random density matrices, and they leave the dependence on the number of parameters and training to future studies.
quotes: We demonstrated the performance of QMINE in estimating the quantum mutual information of random density matrices through numerical simulations of a quantum circuit.
In future, we suggest investigating the specifics of nparams and ntrain pertaining to the quantum neural network problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope and limits.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware run is reported; the stated quantum advantage rests on simulation and argument.

papers.title_in_file: What can we learn from quantum convolutional neural networks?
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 dated December 2024.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, ground-state feature map sections, finite-shot section, discussion, conclusion, one appendix result. Fluid dynamics derivations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: An analysis of why quantum convolutional neural networks recognize quantum phases well, interpreting them through ground-state feature maps, with a fluid dynamics extension.

assertions.value: The authors state that, by analyzing selected examples previously explored with QCNNs, high performance in quantum phase recognition comes from generating a highly effective basis set with sharp features at critical points.
quotes: we show that high performance in quantum phase recognition comes from generating a highly effective basis set with sharp features at critical points.
The learning process adapts the measurement to create sharp decision boundaries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Result from analysis of selected examples in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that 100% test accuracy is still achieved with an arbitrary variational ansatz trained on 4 training points using the ground-state embedding QCNN, and that the sharpness at criticality is maintained.
quotes: we compare the performance of the GS embedding QCNN with the guided and arbitrary variational ansatze in Fig. 8.
We find that 100% test accuracy is still achieved with this arbitrary ansatz trained on 4 training points, and the sharpness at criticality is maintained.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a specific model.

assertions.value: The authors report that the performance separation between the ground-state and Fourier embeddings is more apparent in the finite shot regime, after earlier results assumed an infinite number of shots.
assertions.anchor: Section on generalization and finite shots, Fig. 6, page 8
quotes: The results so far assumed access to an infinite number of shots when measuring expectation values
The separation in the performance between the GS and Fourier embeddings is even more apparent when we move to the finite shot regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that using ground-state embeddings for multiple features requires assigning each feature to some Hamiltonian parameter, and that finding datasets of limited-entanglement states that keep trainability guarantees is an open challenge.
quotes: Once we want to use ground state embeddings for multiple features, we face a task of assigning each feature
Maintaining the trainability guarantees is also important, hence the entanglement of these quantum states must be limited. Finding such datasets is an open challenge.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope and limits.
assertions.reader_inference: The discussion also acknowledges work showing some QCNNs live in a polynomial operator subspace and may be classically treatable, which bears on any quantum advantage claim.

assertions.value: The authors present the variational separability verifier (VSV), a variational quantum algorithm that determines the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt distance.
quotes: We present the variational separability verifier (VSV), which is a novel variational quantum algorithm (VQA) that determines the closest separable state (CSS) of an arbitrary quantum state with respect to the Hilbert
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method.

assertions.value: The authors state they assessed convergence of the VSV optimization for GHZ states of up to seven qubits, using both statevector and shot-based simulations.
quotes: states of up to seven qubits, using both statevector and shot-based simulations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup and scope.
